The quote is verbatim apart from the marked ellipses and quo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: East Limba (Wara Wara dialect) is described as a tone language: a basic High/Low lexical contrast (plus rising, falling and downstepped H) carried by nouns, adverbs/ideophones and most affixes, with verb and adjective roots lexically toneless and receiving grammatical tone; the source says nothing about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning stress. Tonal notes: syllabic nasal prefixes are not lexically contrastive for tone (surface L) but can bear grammatical H; downstep after H vs rising elsewhere in complementary distribution; the West-Central Tonko dialect (not East Limba) has utterance-final H-lowering, which 'clearly does not apply in the northern dialects' (Hyman & Kamara 2025 fn.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone plus grammatical tone in phrases/clauses; citation forms and phrasal contexts both given. No stress domain stated because no stress is described.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Limba-Wara Wara dialect of Kabala/Yagala (Koinadugu), i.e. Glottolog 'Northern Limba' [nort2763] under East Limba [east2387]; Rolle's own CV links his Limba fieldwork to east2387. The handouts also cite parallel Limba-Tonko data (Hyman & Kamara), which is West-Central Limba [west2450]; the Hyman & Kamara 2025 papers saved here are Tonko only. Older work (Clarke 1922, Berry 1958, Mukarovsky 1962/63) is on the southern Biriwa/Safroko cluster, which Glottolog files partly under east2387 (Clarke, Berry) and partly under west2450 (Mukarovsky).

The word as it was pronounced in isolation is provided, including its tone pattern. Sometimes a final HH sequence is HM, but this corresponds underlyingly in most cases to /HH/ in the phonology. For verbs, this is mostly the imperative form, and for nouns it is forms in singular reference. " [CODES file:] LEXICAL_TONE ... "proposed underlying tone pattern based on behavior in context, and from isolation pronunciation" ... H=high; L=low; D=downstepped high; ?=uncertain; 0=underlyingly toneless; *=continuous stretch of H/L tone

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Rolle 2024 handout statement (tone language, H/L with downstep, lexical tone on all nouns; no stress statement): the primary field materials behind that handout mark tone only and never mention stress. The DOI resolves to CLA collection 2022-06 'Limba Field Materials' (collid 11303), not '2022-13' as the citation says; dialect stated in ABOUT as Wara Wara, locations Kabala and Yagala, main consultants Kondeh Mansaray, Albert Korloi Sesay, Kondowulay Marah. Remaining 24 items are m4a/wav/mov recordings and jpg photos with no text files (checked via each item's Box folder listing); not downloaded.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule: the collection records lexical tone only. The ABOUT file says the data 'focused on the sound system and tone' and give each word's isolation tone pattern; the CODES file defines LEXICAL_TONE as H = high, L = low, D = downstepped high, 0 = underlyingly toneless, * = continuous stretch of H/L. Neither the ~990-lexeme spreadsheet nor the two handwritten field notebooks (read page by page) contain the words stress, accent or prominence; all prosodic remarks are about tone (H/L, downstep, rising, 'H tone spread', 'tone hard to determine', 'must be downstepped'), vowel length and nasalisation.
new_statements.exceptions: none (tone notes only: 'Sometimes a final HH sequence is HM'; notebook remarks on downstep, rising tone, H-spread and toneless items)
new_statements.identity_note: The CLA collection (ABOUT file: 'Dialect: Wara Wara', 'Location: Kalaba [sic, Kabala] and Yagala, Sierra Leone') is exactly the East Limba / Wara Wara variety of Kabala-Yagala that east2387 names; the red notebook also has one page of comparison forms from a Kasonko (Sella Limba area) speaker (2022-05-01, 'from Kasonko Sira Kamara'), marked as such. The citation's 'collection 2022-13' is the CLA's 2022-06; same DOI.
